A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Jacobian SAE research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original Pythia experiments measuring Jacobian sparsity, reconstruction, interpretability, randomized-model controls, and intervention responses, with additional analyses and examples in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports additional global-sparsity results and revised qualitative analyses of output latents and their associated inputs.

M1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds a proposed GLU adaptation with a gating-specific Jacobian calculation; v1 only suggested this extension as future work. The evaluated TopK SAE architecture, reconstruction-plus-Jacobian loss, and training procedure remain unchanged. No GLU experiments are reported.

E1.justification: Both versions train on the Pile excluding Books3 and evaluate on C4. The revised qualitative examples use the same first 10K English-subset records. Language-related features discovered within these records do not constitute a new language benchmark; German examples already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: The norm comparison expands from traditional SAEs and JSAEs on a pretrained model in v1 Figure 31 to include Traditional (Randomized) and JSAE (Randomized) controls in v2 Figure 35. These controls were already present in other experiments, but are newly included in this comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds a full-matrix sparsity protocol that averages Jacobians across tokens, conditioning on output-latent activity, alongside the existing tokenwise evaluation. Its qualitative protocol changes from selecting latent pairs and Jacobian-maximizing snippets to selecting outputs, influential inputs, and activation-maximizing snippets. The norm analysis also changes its stated Pythia-70m layer from 4 to 3.

E4.justification: Figure 36 newly tests whether sparsity persists when connections are aggregated across inputs. Section 5.2 and Appendix C substantially rework the individual-pair case studies into output-centered computational examples. The norm diagnostic gains randomized controls, while v1's exploratory activation/Jacobian correlation analysis is removed. Existing sensitivity and linearity analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both retain the ten-repeat timing comparison and its standard-deviation reporting. Neither adds seed-based uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance testing. Revised latent-level means, counts, and standard deviations change the reported results rather than introducing a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 reports global-sparsity findings and substantially revised qualitative results in Figures 18–20; output latent 64386 from v1 reappears under different example selection. Norm values change with the reported layer setting and added controls, so they are not same-setting gains. v1's Table 1 and approximately 0.1 correlation observation disappear. Main reconstruction results and the 97.7% intervention-agreement finding remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds GLU equations, product-rule derivatives, and an active-submatrix Jacobian formula in Equations 17–29. This is a limited mathematical extension beyond v1's GPT-2-style MLP derivation; the existing derivation and approximate-linearity definitions are retained.

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion newly claim that JSAEs discover highly interpretable computations with identifiable input concepts for output concepts. v1 described interpreting feature pairs as difficult and deferred further investigation. The abstract and central efficiency, sparsity, reconstruction, and learned-structure claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds functional interpretations involving German-text detection and grammatical uses of 'do', replacing v1's more cautious discussion of pair interpretation. Section 5.4 also explicitly qualifies the linearity evidence because reconstruction error for a fitted linear surrogate was not evaluated. Existing single-layer and TopK limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C documents the revised output/input ranking and example-collection procedure, and Section 5.2 provides a new link to additional qualitative examples. Core training hyperparameters, hardware and timing information, and the source-code link are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Shah et al. and Balasubramanian et al. as related approaches to identifying relevant computation. It removes the Chanin et al. feature-absorption discussion and reference, and the Raffel et al. reference. Positioning relative to SAEs, transcoders, and automated circuit discovery is otherwise retained.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main narrative remain intact. v2 inserts Section 5.2 and Appendix A.1, replaces the former qualitative Appendix F with Appendix C, and makes localized introduction, conclusion, contribution-statement, and conference-format edits. This is not a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds the German-feature schematic and global-sparsity chart, expands the norm plot, and recasts the qualitative tables into extensive multipage output/input figures. The aggregate statistics table is removed. Most other charts retain their content but are renumbered and rearranged.

improvement.justification: Figure 36 strengthens the evidence beyond token-local sparsity, while the GLU derivation and output-centered examples make the approach more concrete. The explicit linear-surrogate caveat improves qualification of the evidence. These gains are limited by handpicked qualitative cases and the loss of v1's weak-correlation observation and aggregate statistics; the central experimental coverage remains unchanged.
